---
title: "Generalized Linear Models"
---

## Introduction {#sec-glm-intro}

The linear model of Chapter 6 assumes a response that is continuous, unbounded, and normally distributed
around a mean that moves on the same scale as the data. Almost none of the outcomes that drive an
indirect treatment comparison (ITC, [Notation](/notation.qmd)) satisfy these assumptions. A clinical trial reports
how many of $n$ randomized patients responded: the outcome is a count of successes out of a fixed
total, bounded between $0$ and $n$, with a variance that shrinks to zero as the success probability
approaches either endpoint. A safety analysis reports the number of adverse events in a fixed
person-time of follow-up: a nonnegative integer whose variance grows with its mean. A survival analysis
reports event times and censoring. For each of these the normal linear model is not merely inefficient;
it is structurally wrong. Fitting a straight line to a probability produces fitted values outside
$[0,1]$, and assuming constant variance contradicts the arithmetic of a binomial or a Poisson count.

Generalized linear models (GLMs) repair this in a single, unified stroke. They keep the central idea of
the linear model, a linear predictor $\eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ that carries all the
covariate information, but they separate it cleanly from two other choices: the probability law of the
response, and the scale on which the mean is linear. The probability law is taken from a single rich
family, the exponential dispersion family, which contains the normal, Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, and
gamma distributions as special cases and ties each one's variance to its mean through a fixed variance
function. The scale is fixed by a *link function* $g$ that maps the mean $\mu_i$ to the linear predictor,
$g(\mu_i) = \eta_i$. Choosing the normal law and the identity link $g(\mu)=\mu$ returns exactly the
linear model of Chapter 6. Choosing the Bernoulli law and the logit link returns logistic regression and
the odds ratio. Choosing the Poisson law and the log link returns Poisson regression and the rate ratio.

This chapter matters for indirect comparison for three reasons, each of which is developed in a later
part of the book and seeded here. First, network meta-analysis (Chapters 13 to 15) and multilevel
network meta-regression (Chapters 20 to 23) write the linear predictor of every trial arm as a GLM and
combine evidence on the *link scale*, almost always the log-odds or log-rate scale; the algebra of this
chapter is the algebra those methods run. Second, the maximum likelihood machinery developed here, the
score equations, Fisher scoring, and iteratively reweighted least squares, is the numerical engine
underneath every fitted outcome model in the book, and its large-sample distribution theory (which we
import from Chapter 5) is what turns a point estimate into a confidence interval. Third, and most
consequential for what follows, the nonlinearity of the link creates a phenomenon with no analogue in
the linear model: the *non-collapsibility* of the odds ratio and the hazard ratio. A treatment effect
that is identical in every stratum of a covariate can differ from the effect computed on the marginal,
population-averaged risks, even with no confounding whatsoever. This single fact forces the distinction
between conditional and marginal estimands that organizes Chapters 11, 17, and 19, and we prove it here
with an explicit two-stratum example whose every number the reader can check by hand.

The development is self-contained and proves everything. It rests on the probability of Chapter 4 (the
exponential family members, the moment and cumulant generating functions of @def-mgf and
@thm-mgf-moments, Jensen's inequality @thm-jensen), the inference of Chapter 5 (the score @def-score, the
Fisher information @def-fisher-information, the information equality @thm-information-equality, and
above all the asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality),
and the least-squares linear algebra of Chapter 6 (the normal equations @thm-ols-normal-equations and
the projection geometry of @def-hat-matrix). The two primary references are @mccullagh1989glm, the
canonical monograph on the subject, and @dias2018nma, which casts the entire ITC enterprise as a
collection of linked GLMs.

::: {.remark}
## A note on reused symbols
This chapter uses four symbols whose meaning the reader should hold distinct from a neighboring use
elsewhere in the book. The natural parameter of the exponential family is written
$\theta$; it is a specific instance of the generic statistical parameter $\boldsymbol\theta$ of Chapter
5, and it is not the subscripted outcome-scale mean $\theta_{ijk}=g^{-1}(\eta_{ijk})$ that the
network-model chapters use. The dispersion parameter is written $\phi$; when the standard normal density
is needed (only in the discussion of the probit link) it is written as the derivative $\Phi'$ of the
standard normal distribution function $\Phi$, so the symbol $\phi$ is never overloaded inside this
chapter. The GLM mean is always written $\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i]$. Finally the letter $\nu$ does double
duty: it is the **reference measure** in the definition of the exponential dispersion family (a single
piece of bookkeeping that lets one formula cover both continuous and discrete responses; explained in
plain terms in @sec-edf), and, separately, the **shape parameter** of the gamma distribution in
@exm-edf-members. The two never appear in the same display, so no formula mixes them. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## GLM objects and scales: a first trial example {#sec-glm-map}

The single hardest thing about a first encounter with GLMs is not any one proof; it is keeping track of
how many different *scales* a single number can live on. A trial reports a count, the model predicts a
mean, the mathematics works internally with a natural parameter, the regression part lives on a linear
predictor, and the effect a clinician reads off is a ratio. These are five different scales for what is,
morally, one fitted quantity. Before any formal definitions we therefore introduce one concrete trial,
label every object on it, and collect the symbols in a table. Every later section is an instruction for
moving between the columns of that table, and we return to this example at each transition.

**Why a single family.** One could, in principle, build the binary-outcome model, the count model, and
the survival model separately, each with its own likelihood, its own estimating equation, and its own
software. The exponential dispersion family (EDF), defined in @sec-edf, is the device that makes this
unnecessary. It is a template: a single algebraic form, @eq-edf-density, into which the normal,
Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, and gamma distributions all fit. The payoff is leverage. Because they share
the template, one mean-variance theorem (@thm-glm-mean-variance), one score equation
(@thm-glm-score), and one fitting algorithm (@thm-irls) serve all of them at once. Proving a fact about
the template proves it simultaneously for logistic regression, Poisson regression, and ordinary linear
regression. That is why the abstraction is worth the price of admission.

::: {#exm-glm-running}
## A running trial: one binary arm and one count arm
Consider a single arm of a clinical trial in which $n=60$ patients are randomized and $R=18$ of them
respond. We will reuse these numbers throughout the chapter.

*The binary (response) outcome.* We record the **proportion** who responded, $y=R/n=18/60=0.30$. The
model's job is to estimate the underlying response **probability** $\mu=p$. The proportion does not live
on the same scale as the probability's regression: a probability is trapped in the interval $(0,1)$,
whereas a regression $\eta=\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ ranges over all of $\mathbb R$. The **link**
$g(\mu)=\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ (the logit) is the strictly increasing change of scale that carries the
probability onto the whole real line, so that $\eta=g(\mu)$ can be modeled linearly. If the arm receives
treatment, coded by an indicator $x=1$, its coefficient $\beta_1$ is a **log odds ratio** and $e^{\beta_1}$
is the **odds ratio** a meta-analysis would combine. The natural variability of the proportion is
$\mathrm{Var}(y)=p(1-p)/n$: largest near $p=\tfrac12$, vanishing as $p$ approaches $0$ or $1$.

*The count (adverse-event) outcome.* Suppose the same arm accrues $7$ adverse events over $t=50$
person-years. Here the response is the **count** $y=7$, the model estimates the expected count
$\mu=\lambda$, and the natural variability is $\mathrm{Var}(y)=\lambda$ (a Poisson count's variance
equals its mean). The link is the **log**, $g(\mu)=\log\mu$, which keeps the fitted mean positive; the
known exposure enters as an **offset** $\log t$, and a treatment coefficient $\beta_1$ is then a **log
rate ratio**, with $e^{\beta_1}$ the incidence rate ratio. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The objects just named, and the scale each one lives on, are collected below. This local map is the
chapter in miniature; the formal definitions that follow simply make each row precise.

| Symbol | Name | Role (what it does) | In the binary trial arm |
|---|---|---|---|
| $Y_i,\;y_i$ | response | the observed data for unit or group $i$ | proportion $y=R/n=0.30$ |
| $\mu_i=\mathbb E[Y_i]$ | mean | what the model predicts, on the data's own scale | response probability $p$ |
| $\theta$ | natural parameter | the EDF's internal coordinate; tunes the distribution | $\log\frac{p}{1-p}$ |
| $b(\theta)$ | cumulant function | the EDF normalizer; its derivatives give mean and variance | $\log(1+e^\theta)$ |
| $\phi$ | dispersion | overall variance scale; equals $1$ for binomial and Poisson | $1$ |
| $w_i$ | prior weight | a known multiplicity, *not* a Bayesian prior; here the denominator | $w=n=60$ |
| $V(\mu)$ | variance function | how the variance depends on the mean | $\mu(1-\mu)$ |
| $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ | linear predictor | the regression part; ranges over all of $\mathbb R$ | $\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i$ |
| $g$ | link | strictly increasing map from the mean scale to the $\eta$ scale | logit $\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ |
| $g^{-1}$ | inverse link | recovers the mean from the linear predictor | $e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)$ |
| $\boldsymbol\beta$ | coefficients | the unknowns estimated from data | $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$; $e^{\beta_1}=$ odds ratio |

Reading down the table is the same as touring the five scales: the **data** scale ($y$), the **mean**
scale ($\mu$, a probability or a rate), the **natural-parameter** scale ($\theta$, the EDF's internal
bookkeeping), the **linear-predictor** or **link** scale ($\eta=g(\mu)$, where the regression lives),
and the **ratio** scale reached by exponentiating a coefficient ($e^{\beta_1}$, an odds or rate ratio).

::: {.remark}
## Why trial data arrive as a proportion with a weight
A health researcher usually pictures a trial arm as a two-by-two count: $R$ responders and $n-R$
nonresponders. A GLM consumes the same information in the slightly different shape "response $y=R/n$ with
prior weight $w=n$." The reason is the arithmetic of @exm-glm-running: each of the $n$ patients is an
independent $\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ trial, so their average $y=R/n$ has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)/n$. The
denominator $n$ is not data to be modeled; it is a *known* multiplier that says how much each proportion
should count, and it is exactly the prior weight $w_i$. Concretely, $R=18$ of $n=60$ gives $y=0.30$,
$w=60$, mean $\mu=p$, and $\mathrm{Var}(y)=p(1-p)/60$. Trial-level ITC data almost always take this
grouped form, one proportion-and-weight pair per arm, which is why we carry the weight $w$ through every
formula. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The exponential dispersion family {#sec-edf}

The random component of a GLM is a member of the following family. The definition is stated once for
both continuous and discrete responses, and the only price of that economy is a single symbol, the
**reference measure** $\nu$. Operationally $\nu$ is nothing more exotic than a reminder of how to add up:
for a continuous response (the normal, the gamma) "integrate against $\nu$" means ordinary integration
$\int f(y)\,dy$, and for a discrete response (the Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson) it means summation
$\sum_y f(y)$ over the possible values. A reader who has never met measure theory can mentally replace
every $\int(\cdot)\,\nu(dy)$ by "integrate if continuous, sum if discrete" and lose nothing; the unified
notation exists only so that the mean-variance theorem and the score equation below need to be proved
once rather than twice. With that understanding we fix $\nu$ to be Lebesgue measure (ordinary $dy$) for
continuous responses and counting measure on the integers (a sum) for discrete ones.

::: {#def-exponential-family}
## Exponential dispersion family
A random variable $Y$ taking values in a set $\mathcal Y\subseteq\mathbb R$ belongs to the
**exponential dispersion family** (EDF) with **natural parameter** $\theta$, **dispersion parameter**
$\phi>0$, and known **prior weight** $w>0$ if its density (or probability mass function) with respect to
$\nu$ has the form
$$
f(y;\theta,\phi) \;=\; \exp\!\left\{\frac{y\,\theta - b(\theta)}{a(\phi)} \;+\; c(y,\phi)\right\},
\qquad a(\phi)=\frac{\phi}{w},
$$ {#eq-edf-density}
where:

(i) the **cumulant function** $b:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ is twice continuously differentiable with
$b''(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta$ in the interior of $\Theta$, and does not depend on $\phi$;

(ii) the **natural parameter space**
$\Theta=\bigl\{\theta\in\mathbb R:\int_{\mathcal Y}\exp(y\theta/a(\phi)+c(y,\phi))\,\nu(dy)<\infty\bigr\}$
is a nonempty open interval;

(iii) $c(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a function not involving $\theta$, chosen so that @eq-edf-density integrates to
one.

We write $Y\sim\mathrm{EDF}(\theta,\phi;w)$. When $w=1$ we write $\mathrm{EDF}(\theta,\phi)$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* The formula @eq-edf-density looks forbidding, but it has only three moving parts and
each plays a single role. The term $y\theta$ **couples the data to the parameter**: it is the one place
where the observation $y$ multiplies the unknown $\theta$, and it is what makes $\theta$ learnable from
$y$. The term $-b(\theta)$ **normalizes**: it is whatever is needed to make the total probability equal
one, and the next theorem shows it secretly stores the mean and variance. The term $c(y,\phi)$
**collects the leftovers** that depend on the data and the dispersion but not on $\theta$; because it is
free of $\theta$ it will drop out of every score equation and never touch $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. The
dispersion $\phi$ and the weight $w$ enter only through $a(\phi)=\phi/w$, an overall divisor of the
exponent. Despite its name, the **prior weight** $w$ is not a Bayesian prior: it is a known multiplicity,
typically the binomial denominator $n_i$ of a trial arm as in @exm-glm-running.

Condition (iii) can be made explicit. The density @eq-edf-density must integrate to $1$ over $\mathcal Y$;
since the factor $\exp\{-b(\theta)/a(\phi)\}$ is constant in $y$ it pulls outside the integral, and
clearing it to the other side shows that for every $\theta\in\Theta$,
$$
\int_{\mathcal Y}\exp\!\left\{\frac{y\,\theta}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}\nu(dy)
\;=\;\exp\!\left\{\frac{b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}\right\}.
$$ {#eq-edf-normalization}
Equivalently, $b(\theta)=a(\phi)\log\int_{\mathcal Y}\exp(y\theta/a(\phi)+c(y,\phi))\,\nu(dy)$; the
defining requirement that a single cumulant function $b$ serve all dispersions $\phi$ is what the word
"dispersion" in the name records, and it holds for every example we use. Identity @eq-edf-normalization
is the engine of the next theorem.

The exponential dispersion family is genuinely a family of distributions, one for each pair
$(\theta,\phi)$; varying $\theta$ moves the mean, and varying $\phi$ scales the variance without
changing the mean, as we now prove.

Before the general theorem, it helps to watch the template @eq-edf-density absorb one distribution
slowly, with every term named.

::: {#exm-edf-bernoulli}
## The EDF density for one Bernoulli response, term by term
Let $Y\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ (@def-bernoulli), so $Y\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(Y=1)=p$. Its mass function
$p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$, rewritten through its logarithm, is
$$
p^y(1-p)^{1-y}=\exp\Bigl\{\,y\underbrace{\log\tfrac{p}{1-p}}_{=\,\theta}\;+\;\underbrace{\log(1-p)}_{=\,-b(\theta)}\,\Bigr\}.
$$
Matching this to @eq-edf-density term by term gives the whole decomposition. The **natural parameter** is
$\theta=\log\frac{p}{1-p}$, the log odds, so $p=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)$. The **cumulant function** is
$b(\theta)=-\log(1-p)=\log(1+e^\theta)$, using $1-p=1/(1+e^\theta)$. The **dispersion** is $\phi=1$ and
the **weight** is $w=1$, so $a(\phi)=1$. The **leftover** term is $c(y,\phi)=0$: nothing is left over,
because a single Bernoulli mass function has no data-only factor to absorb. Differentiating $b$ already
previews the theorem below: $b'(\theta)=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)=p=\mu$ returns the mean, and
$b''(\theta)=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)^2=p(1-p)$ returns the variance function $V(\mu)=\mu(1-\mu)$. The single
binary patient of @exm-glm-running is exactly this object, with $p$ the response probability.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Mean and variance from the cumulant function

The single most useful fact about the EDF is that its mean and variance are read off from the
derivatives of $b$. Two objects with nearly identical names appear here and must be kept apart: the
**cumulant function** $b(\theta)$ is the fixed piece of the density @eq-edf-density, a property of the
distribution, whereas the **cumulant generating function** $K_Y(t)=\log\mathbb E[e^{tY}]$ is a tool we
build from $Y$ to extract its moments. They share the word "cumulant" because, as the proof shows, the
first controls the second.

*Strategy of the proof.* The mean and variance are the first two **cumulants** of $Y$, and cumulants are
by definition the derivatives of $K_Y$ at $t=0$, so $\mathbb E[Y]=K_Y'(0)$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=K_Y''(0)$. The proof is therefore a two-step plan: first compute $K_Y(t)$ in closed
form, where it turns out to equal $[b(\theta+t\,a(\phi))-b(\theta)]/a(\phi)$, then differentiate it twice
at $0$. A reader who grasps this plan can skip the algebra and still trust the conclusion.

::: {#thm-glm-mean-variance}
## Mean and variance of an EDF response
Let $Y\sim\mathrm{EDF}(\theta,\phi;w)$ with $\theta$ in the interior of $\Theta$, and write
$a(\phi)=\phi/w$. Then the moment generating function of $Y$ is finite in a neighborhood of the origin
and
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=b'(\theta)=:\mu,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)\,b''(\theta)=\frac{\phi}{w}\,b''(\theta).
$$ {#eq-glm-mean-variance}
Moreover the map $\theta\mapsto\mu=b'(\theta)$ is a strictly increasing bijection from the interior of
$\Theta$ onto an open interval $\mathcal M\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **mean space**; its inverse is written
$\theta(\mu)$, and the **variance function**
$$
V(\mu):=b''\bigl(\theta(\mu)\bigr)>0
$$ {#eq-variance-function}
expresses the variance as $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)\,V(\mu)$, a known function of the mean times the
dispersion.
:::

*Why this matters.* Equation @eq-glm-mean-variance is the lever the rest of the chapter pulls. Once the
cumulant function $b$ of a distribution is known, its mean and its whole variance structure follow by
differentiation alone, with no further integration. The same cumulant-function trick reappears in the
score equation (@thm-glm-score), the Fisher information (@prp-glm-information), and the large-sample
theory (@cor-glm-asymptotic-normality), so the work done here is repaid three more times. For an indirect
comparison this is what puts every trial outcome, binary, count, or continuous, on a common footing with
a known mean and variance, the precondition for combining them in a network meta-analysis.

::: {.proof}
Fix $\theta$ interior to $\Theta$. Because $\Theta$ is open, there is $\epsilon>0$ with
$[\theta-\epsilon a(\phi),\,\theta+\epsilon a(\phi)]\subseteq\Theta$. The substitution that drives the
computation is $\theta'=\theta+t\,a(\phi)$: it is chosen precisely so that the extra factor $e^{ty}$ from
the moment generating function merges into the natural-parameter term of the density, because in the
exponent
$$
ty+\frac{y\theta}{a(\phi)}=\frac{y\bigl(\theta+t\,a(\phi)\bigr)}{a(\phi)}=\frac{y\theta'}{a(\phi)}.
$$
For $|t|<\epsilon$ put $\theta'=\theta+t\,a(\phi)\in\Theta$ and compute the moment generating function
$M_Y(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tY}]$ (@def-mgf) directly from @eq-edf-density:
$$
M_Y(t)=\int_{\mathcal Y}e^{ty}\exp\!\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}\nu(dy)
=e^{-b(\theta)/a(\phi)}\int_{\mathcal Y}\exp\!\left\{\frac{y\theta'}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}\nu(dy).
$$
The integral on the right is finite because $\theta'\in\Theta$, and by the normalization identity
@eq-edf-normalization applied at $\theta'$ it equals $\exp\{b(\theta')/a(\phi)\}$. Hence, for
$|t|<\epsilon$,
$$
M_Y(t)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{b(\theta+t\,a(\phi))-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}\right\}<\infty.
$$
The moment generating function is therefore finite on a neighborhood of $0$, and the **cumulant
generating function** $K_Y(t)=\log M_Y(t)$ is
$$
K_Y(t)=\frac{b(\theta+t\,a(\phi))-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}.
$$ {#eq-edf-cgf}
Since $b$ is twice continuously differentiable on the open set $\Theta$, so is $K_Y$ near $0$, with
$$
K_Y'(t)=b'(\theta+t\,a(\phi)),\qquad K_Y''(t)=a(\phi)\,b''(\theta+t\,a(\phi)).
$$
Now relate the derivatives of $K_Y$ at $0$ to the mean and variance. Because $M_Y$ is finite near $0$ it
is infinitely differentiable there with $M_Y(0)=1$, $M_Y'(0)=\mathbb E[Y]$, and $M_Y''(0)=\mathbb E[Y^2]$
(@thm-mgf-moments). From $K_Y=\log M_Y$,
$$
K_Y'=\frac{M_Y'}{M_Y},\qquad K_Y''=\frac{M_Y''M_Y-(M_Y')^2}{M_Y^2},
$$
so at $t=0$, using $M_Y(0)=1$,
$$
K_Y'(0)=M_Y'(0)=\mathbb E[Y],\qquad
K_Y''(0)=M_Y''(0)-\bigl(M_Y'(0)\bigr)^2=\mathbb E[Y^2]-\bigl(\mathbb E[Y]\bigr)^2=\mathrm{Var}(Y).
$$
Evaluating the two displayed derivatives of @eq-edf-cgf at $t=0$ gives $\mathbb E[Y]=b'(\theta)$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta)$, which is @eq-glm-mean-variance.

For the second claim, $b''>0$ on the interior of $\Theta$ makes $b'$ strictly increasing there, hence
injective, and continuous. Its image $\mathcal M$ is an interval, because a continuous function carries an
interval to an interval (the intermediate value theorem: every value lying between two attained values is
itself attained). That interval is moreover *open*: a strictly increasing function on an open interval
attains neither a largest nor a smallest value, since any candidate extreme point has a still-smaller or
still-larger neighbor inside the domain, so $\mathcal M$ contains none of its endpoints. Thus
$b':\mathrm{int}\,\Theta\to\mathcal M$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection with continuous
inverse $\theta(\cdot)$. Define $V(\mu)=b''(\theta(\mu))$; it is positive because $b''>0$, and
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta)=a(\phi)V(\mu)$ by substituting $\theta=\theta(\mu)$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Why the variance is tied to the mean
Equation @eq-glm-mean-variance is the structural heart of the GLM. In the normal model the variance
$\phi$ is free of the mean, but in every other member of the family the variance is forced to be
$a(\phi)V(\mu)$ with $V$ fixed by the distribution. For the Bernoulli law $V(\mu)=\mu(1-\mu)$, so the
variance must vanish at the endpoints; for the Poisson law $V(\mu)=\mu$, so the variance must equal the
mean. For a trial this is not bookkeeping: the uncertainty in a response probability near $\tfrac12$
genuinely exceeds that near $0$ or $1$, and the scatter of an event count genuinely grows with its
expected size, so tying the variance to the mean is what lets a GLM report honest standard errors. A GLM
does not get to choose the mean-variance relationship independently of the response
distribution, and this is exactly the discipline that a normal linear model on a count or a proportion
lacks. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The standard members

We verify that the distributions named in the introduction are EDF members and record their cumulant
function, dispersion, and variance function. Each verification is a short algebraic rearrangement of the
density into the canonical form @eq-edf-density.

::: {#exm-edf-members}
## Five exponential dispersion families
**Normal.** For $Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ ([Notation](/notation.qmd)), expand the density:
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}
=\exp\!\left\{\frac{y\mu-\mu^2/2}{\sigma^2}-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2}-\tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)\right\}.
$$
This is @eq-edf-density with $\theta=\mu$, $b(\theta)=\theta^2/2$, $\phi=\sigma^2$, $w=1$, and
$c(y,\phi)=-y^2/(2\phi)-\tfrac12\log(2\pi\phi)$. Then $b'(\theta)=\theta=\mu$ and $b''(\theta)=1$, so
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\phi=\sigma^2$ and $V(\mu)=1$: the variance is constant, as it must be.

**Bernoulli.** For $Y\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p)$ (@def-bernoulli),
$p^y(1-p)^{1-y}=\exp\{y\log\frac{p}{1-p}+\log(1-p)\}$. Set $\theta=\log\frac{p}{1-p}$, so
$p=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)$ and $\log(1-p)=-\log(1+e^\theta)$. Thus $b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta)$,
$\phi=1$, $w=1$, $c\equiv0$. Here $b'(\theta)=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)=p=\mu$ and
$b''(\theta)=e^\theta/(1+e^\theta)^2=p(1-p)$, so $V(\mu)=\mu(1-\mu)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu(1-\mu)$.

**Binomial proportion.** For a grouped binomial response $Y=R/n$ with $R\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$
(@def-binomial), the proportion has the same $\theta=\log\frac{p}{1-p}$ and $b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta)$
as the Bernoulli, but with prior weight $w=n$ and $\phi=1$, so $a(\phi)=1/n$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu(1-\mu)/n$. The grouped form is what trial-level ITC data take.

**Poisson.** For $Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$ (@def-poisson),
$e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y/y!=\exp\{y\log\lambda-\lambda-\log y!\}$. Set $\theta=\log\lambda$, so
$b(\theta)=e^\theta=\lambda$, $\phi=1$, $w=1$, $c(y,\phi)=-\log y!$. Then $b'(\theta)=e^\theta=\lambda=\mu$
and $b''(\theta)=e^\theta=\lambda$, so $V(\mu)=\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu$: variance equals mean.

**Gamma.** For $Y$ gamma with mean $\mu$ and shape $\nu$, density
$\frac{1}{\Gamma(\nu)}(\nu/\mu)^\nu y^{\nu-1}e^{-\nu y/\mu}$, write the exponent as
$\frac{y(-1/\mu)+\log\mu}{1/\nu}+(\nu-1)\log y+\nu\log\nu-\log\Gamma(\nu)$. Set $\theta=-1/\mu<0$, so
$b(\theta)=-\log(-\theta)=\log\mu$, $\phi=1/\nu$, $w=1$. Then $b'(\theta)=-1/\theta=\mu$ and
$b''(\theta)=1/\theta^2=\mu^2$, giving $V(\mu)=\mu^2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu^2/\nu$: constant
coefficient of variation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The five members are summarized below; the canonical link in the last column is defined in
@sec-links.

| Distribution | $\theta(\mu)$ | $b(\theta)$ | $\phi$ | $V(\mu)$ | canonical link $g(\mu)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | $\mu$ | $\theta^2/2$ | $\sigma^2$ | $1$ | identity $\mu$ |
| Bernoulli/Binomial | $\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ | $\log(1+e^\theta)$ | $1$ | $\mu(1-\mu)$ | logit $\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ |
| Poisson | $\log\mu$ | $e^\theta$ | $1$ | $\mu$ | log $\log\mu$ |
| Gamma | $-1/\mu$ | $-\log(-\theta)$ | $1/\nu$ | $\mu^2$ | reciprocal $-1/\mu$ |

The theorem introduced the **mean space** $\mathcal M$, which deserves a plain reading: it is simply the
set of values the mean is allowed to take for the distribution at hand. For the Bernoulli and binomial it
is the open interval $(0,1)$, the range of a probability; for the Poisson and gamma it is $(0,\infty)$,
the range of a positive rate or mean; for the normal it is all of $\mathbb R$. The link function, defined
next, is a change of scale that acts exactly on $\mathcal M$.

## Link functions and the generalized linear model {#sec-links}

The EDF supplies the random component. The systematic component is the familiar linear predictor
$\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$. The link function is the bridge between them.

::: {#def-link-function}
## Link function
A **link function** is a function $g:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R$ defined on the mean space $\mathcal M$ of an
EDF that is twice continuously differentiable and strictly monotone, hence a bijection from $\mathcal M$
onto an open interval $g(\mathcal M)\subseteq\mathbb R$. Its inverse $g^{-1}$, called the **mean
function** or **response function**, recovers the mean from the linear predictor. A generalized linear
model relates the mean of the $i$-th response to its linear predictor by
$$
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\mu_i=g^{-1}(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta).
$$ {#eq-link}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* A link is just a relabeling of the mean onto the regression scale. It takes a mean
$\mu$, which may be confined to a probability in $(0,1)$ or a positive rate in $(0,\infty)$, and reports a
number $\eta=g(\mu)$ that is free to be any real, so the linear predictor $\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta$
can equal it without running into a boundary. The logit turns a probability into a log odds; the log
turns a rate into a log rate. Inverting the link, $\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)$, turns a fitted linear predictor back
into a legal mean.

Strict monotonicity is exactly what guarantees that $g$ can be inverted, so that every value of the
linear predictor names exactly one mean; and because $g$ is strictly monotone and continuous on the open
interval $\mathcal M$, its image $g(\mathcal M)$ is again an open interval (the same argument that made
$\mathcal M$ open above), which is what lets the unrestricted linear predictor range over it freely. The
twice-differentiability requirement is the one clause a beginner does not need yet: it is invisible until
the estimation theory of @sec-glm-estimation, where the fitting algorithm differentiates the link twice;
until then it can be read as "smooth enough." Among all links for a given EDF, one is distinguished.

::: {#def-canonical-link}
## Canonical link
The **canonical link** (or natural link) of an EDF is $g_{\mathrm{c}}=(b')^{-1}=\theta(\cdot)$, the
inverse of the mean map of @thm-glm-mean-variance. It is a valid link function: $b'$ is a strictly
increasing $C^1$ bijection from $\mathrm{int}\,\Theta$ onto $\mathcal M$ by @thm-glm-mean-variance, so
$\theta(\cdot)=g_{\mathrm c}$ is a strictly increasing $C^1$ bijection from $\mathcal M$ onto
$\mathrm{int}\,\Theta$, and it is $C^2$ because $b'$ is $C^2$ with nonvanishing derivative $b''>0$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* Of the many links one could attach to a distribution, the canonical link is the one
that coincides with the distribution's own natural parameter $\theta$. Choosing it is a convenience worth
understanding now for one reason and trusting for another: it makes the estimation algorithm simplest
(proved in @sec-glm-estimation), and for the families health researchers use it also yields the
interpretable effect measures, the logit giving the odds ratio and the log giving the rate ratio. It is a
sensible default, not an obligation.

::: {#prp-canonical-eta-theta}
## The canonical link identifies the linear predictor with the natural parameter
A GLM uses its canonical link if and only if the natural parameter equals the linear predictor for every
observation: $\theta_i=\eta_i$.
:::

::: {.proof}
With the canonical link, $\eta_i=g_{\mathrm c}(\mu_i)=\theta(\mu_i)=\theta(b'(\theta_i))=\theta_i$, the
last step because $\theta(\cdot)$ inverts $b'$. Conversely, if $\theta_i=\eta_i=g(\mu_i)$ for the link in
use, then $g(\mu_i)=\theta_i=\theta(\mu_i)$ for all attainable $\mu_i$, so $g=\theta(\cdot)=g_{\mathrm c}$
on $\mathcal M$. $\square$
:::

*Why this matters.* The identity $\theta_i=\eta_i$ is precisely why the canonical link makes the
mathematics clean: the natural parameter, the EDF's internal coordinate, and the linear predictor, the
regression, become one and the same object, collapsing the chain of scales in @sec-glm-map by a link.
This single coincidence produces the simple score equation of @cor-canonical-score and the global
concavity of @lem-canonical-hessian, and it is why logistic and Poisson regression, both canonical, are
the workhorses on which network meta-analysis is built.

Reading the canonical-link column of the table in @sec-edf confirms the familiar choices: the identity
link for the normal, the **logit** link $g(\mu)=\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ for the Bernoulli and binomial,
the **log** link $g(\mu)=\log\mu$ for the Poisson, and the reciprocal link $-1/\mu$ for the gamma. The
canonical link is not mandatory, and @sec-links below introduces the probit and complementary log-log
links for binary data, but it confers the analytic and computational simplifications proved in
@sec-glm-estimation.

We can now state the object of study precisely.

::: {#def-glm}
## Generalized linear model
A **generalized linear model** for independent responses $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ with known covariate vectors
$\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ (the rows of the design matrix
$\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$) and known prior weights $w_1,\dots,w_n>0$ consists of three
components:

1. **Random component.** Each $Y_i\sim\mathrm{EDF}(\theta_i,\phi;w_i)$ independently, with the same
cumulant function $b$ and dispersion $\phi$ across $i$, so that by @thm-glm-mean-variance
$\mu_i=\mathbb E[Y_i]=b'(\theta_i)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=a_i(\phi)V(\mu_i)$ with $a_i(\phi)=\phi/w_i$.

2. **Systematic component.** A linear predictor $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ with unknown
coefficient vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p$.

3. **Link.** A link function $g$ (@def-link-function) with $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$.

The normal linear model of Chapter 6 (@def-linear-model) is the special case in which the random
component is normal and the link is the identity. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* A GLM is assembled from three independent choices, and naming all three specifies
the model completely: pick the response distribution (which fixes the mean-variance link through $V$),
pick the covariates that enter the linear predictor, and pick the link scale. Logistic regression is the
choice (Bernoulli, covariates, logit); Poisson regression is (Poisson, covariates, log); the linear model
of Chapter 6 is (normal, covariates, identity). Everything downstream, the estimate, its standard error,
the model tests, is then computed mechanically. Notice one small notational shift now that several
observations are in play: the single dispersion divisor $a(\phi)$ of @def-exponential-family becomes the
per-observation $a_i(\phi)=\phi/w_i$, differing only through the known weight $w_i$.

### Logistic regression {#sec-logistic}

Take the Bernoulli or binomial random component and the canonical logit link. Writing $p_i=\mu_i$ for
the success probability, the model is
$$
\mathrm{logit}(p_i)=\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
p_i=\frac{e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}}{1+e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}}.
$$ {#eq-logistic}
The inverse link $g^{-1}(\eta)=e^\eta/(1+e^\eta)$ is the standard logistic distribution function; it maps
the whole real line into $(0,1)$, so fitted probabilities are automatically valid. The interpretation of
the coefficients is the reason this model dominates the analysis of binary trial outcomes. The quantity
$p_i/(1-p_i)$ is the **odds** of success, and $\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ is the **log-odds**.
If two observations differ by one unit in covariate $x_j$ and agree on every other covariate, their
log-odds differ by exactly $\beta_j$, so their odds differ by the multiplicative factor $e^{\beta_j}$.
That factor is the **odds ratio** (OR) associated with a unit change in $x_j$:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{odds}(x_j+1)}{\mathrm{odds}(x_j)}
=\frac{p(x_j+1)/(1-p(x_j+1))}{p(x_j)/(1-p(x_j))}=e^{\beta_j}.
$$ {#eq-odds-ratio}
A treatment indicator's coefficient is therefore a log odds ratio, and $e^\beta$ is the odds ratio that
network meta-analysis combines across trials (@dias2018nma, Chapter 4). The conditioning on "every other
covariate held fixed" in this interpretation is precisely the conditional-effect language whose
divergence from the marginal effect we examine in @sec-noncollapsibility. Hold onto the word
*conditional*: this coefficient answers the question "what happens within a fixed covariate profile?",
whereas an indirect comparison often needs a *marginal* answer averaged over a whole trial population, and
@sec-noncollapsibility shows that for the odds ratio these two answers can differ even with no confounding
at all.

### Poisson regression {#sec-poisson}

Take the Poisson random component and the canonical log link. With $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ the mean count,
$$
\log\lambda_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\lambda_i=e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$ {#eq-poisson}
The mean is forced positive, as a count's mean must be. A unit change in $x_j$ multiplies the expected
count by $e^{\beta_j}$, the **rate ratio**. When the observations accrue over different exposures (a
person-time $t_i$ for a rate, or a denominator population for an incidence), one writes
$\lambda_i=t_i\,e^{\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta}$, equivalently
$\log\lambda_i=\log t_i+\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$. The term $\log t_i$ is a known regressor with
coefficient fixed at $1$, called an **offset**; it is not estimated. With an offset the linear predictor
models the log-rate $\log(\lambda_i/t_i)$, and $e^{\beta_j}$ is an incidence rate ratio, the count
analogue of the odds ratio.

### The probit and complementary log-log links {#sec-other-links}

For binary data the logit link is canonical but not the only sensible choice. Two non-canonical links
recur in the ITC literature.

The **probit** link is $g(\mu)=\Phi^{-1}(\mu)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution
function; its inverse link is $g^{-1}(\eta)=\Phi(\eta)$. It arises from a latent-variable model: if an
unobserved $Y_i^\ast=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_i$ with
$\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ crosses zero, $Y_i=\mathbf 1\{Y_i^\ast>0\}$, then
$P(Y_i=1)=P(\varepsilon_i>-\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)=\Phi(\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta)$. The
inverse-link derivative is $\frac{d\mu}{d\eta}=\Phi'(\eta)$, the standard normal density. The probit and
logit fits are numerically very close after rescaling the coefficients, because the logistic and normal
distribution functions are similar in shape; the logit is usually preferred only because its coefficients
carry the exact log odds ratio interpretation of @eq-odds-ratio.

The **complementary log-log** (cloglog) link is $g(\mu)=\log(-\log(1-\mu))$, with inverse link
$g^{-1}(\eta)=1-\exp(-e^\eta)$. Unlike the logit and probit it is asymmetric in $\mu$ and $1-\mu$. It
arises from grouped survival data under a proportional hazards mechanism: if a continuous event time has
hazard multiplied by $e^{\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta}$, the probability of an event within a fixed
interval satisfies $\log(-\log(1-\mu))=\log(-\log S_0)+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ for a baseline
survival $S_0$, exactly a cloglog GLM with offset $\log(-\log S_0)$. This connection to the hazard ratio
is the reason the cloglog link reappears when @sec-noncollapsibility discusses the non-collapsibility of
the hazard ratio.

::: {.remark}
## Why the link scale matters for indirect comparison
The choice of link is not a modeling nicety; it fixes the scale on which an indirect comparison does its
arithmetic. Network meta-analysis and its regression extensions write the linear predictor of every trial
arm as a study baseline plus relative treatment effects, and they add and subtract those effects on the
link scale: the log-odds scale for binary outcomes, the log-rate scale for counts. A Bucher indirect
comparison of treatments $B$ and $C$ through a common comparator $A$ (developed in Chapter 14), for
instance, forms $d_{BC}=d_{AC}-d_{AB}$, subtracting two log odds ratios; the operation is coherent only
because each $d$ lives on the same additive logit scale. The link is thus the common currency of the
whole enterprise, and the conditional, link-scale reading of a coefficient from @sec-logistic is the
reading those methods rely on. The price of that convenience, charged in @sec-noncollapsibility, is that a
link-scale effect need not agree with the effect computed on population-averaged risks.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Maximum likelihood estimation {#sec-glm-estimation}

The coefficient vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ is estimated by maximum likelihood (@def-mle). Because the
responses are independent EDF members, the log-likelihood is a sum of EDF log-densities, and its
maximization has a remarkable structure: the stationarity condition is a weighted version of the normal
equations of Chapter 6, and the Newton-type algorithm that solves it is a sequence of weighted linear
regressions. We derive all of this from @eq-edf-density.

*What the software is doing.* When a health researcher fits a logistic regression, the program is solving
a single optimization problem: find the coefficient vector $\boldsymbol\beta$ that makes the observed
responses most probable under the model. Unlike linear regression, this has no closed-form answer for the
logistic or Poisson likelihood, so the program proceeds in steps. It writes down the condition that the
gradient of the log-likelihood vanishes (the **score equations**), measures the curvature of the
log-likelihood (the **Fisher information**), and walks toward the maximum by a Newton-type update
(**Fisher scoring**) that turns out to be an ordinary weighted least-squares fit (**IRLS**). The four
named results of this section are exactly those four ingredients, in that order; the worked example of
@sec-glm-worked then runs them on real numbers.

Throughout, the log-likelihood of the GLM as a function of $\boldsymbol\beta$ is, dropping the additive
constant $\sum_i c(y_i,\phi)$ that does not involve $\boldsymbol\beta$,
$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)},
\qquad a_i(\phi)=\frac{\phi}{w_i},
$$ {#eq-glm-loglik}
in which each $\theta_i=\theta(\mu_i)$ and $\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)$ and $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$
are functions of $\boldsymbol\beta$ through the chain
$\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto\eta_i\mapsto\mu_i\mapsto\theta_i$.

### The score equations

::: {#thm-glm-score}
## GLM score equations
For the GLM of @def-glm the score function (@def-score) $\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)$
has components
$$
U_j(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{w_i\,(y_i-\mu_i)}{\phi\,V(\mu_i)}\,\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}\,x_{ij},
\qquad j=1,\dots,p,
$$ {#eq-glm-score}
equivalently, in matrix form with $\mathbf D=\mathrm{diag}(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)$ and the response covariance
$\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf Y)=\mathrm{diag}(a_i(\phi)V(\mu_i))$,
$$
\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu).
$$ {#eq-glm-score-matrix}
The maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ solves $\mathbf U(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0$.
The dispersion $\phi$ enters @eq-glm-score only as the overall factor $1/\phi$, so the solution
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ does not depend on $\phi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Differentiate @eq-glm-loglik by the chain rule along $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto\eta_i\mapsto\mu_i\mapsto\theta_i$.
The four links of the chain are:
$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_i}=\frac{y_i-b'(\theta_i)}{a_i(\phi)}=\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{a_i(\phi)},
\qquad
\frac{d\theta_i}{d\mu_i}=\frac{1}{b''(\theta_i)}=\frac{1}{V(\mu_i)},
$$
the first because $\partial_{\theta_i}(y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i))=y_i-b'(\theta_i)$ and $b'(\theta_i)=\mu_i$
by @thm-glm-mean-variance. The second factor unpacks in three short steps: (1) since $\mu_i=b'(\theta_i)$,
differentiating gives $d\mu_i/d\theta_i=b''(\theta_i)$; (2) by the definition @eq-variance-function of the
variance function, $b''(\theta_i)=V(\mu_i)$; (3) the derivative of an inverse function is the reciprocal of
the derivative, so $d\theta_i/d\mu_i=1/(d\mu_i/d\theta_i)=1/V(\mu_i)$. Continuing the chain,
$$
\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}=\bigl(g'(\mu_i)\bigr)^{-1},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\eta_i}{\partial\beta_j}=x_{ij},
$$
the first because $\eta_i=g(\mu_i)$ gives $d\eta_i/d\mu_i=g'(\mu_i)$. Multiplying the four factors and
summing over $i$,
$$
U_j(\boldsymbol\beta)=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_j}
=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{a_i(\phi)}\cdot\frac{1}{V(\mu_i)}\cdot\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}\cdot x_{ij}
=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{w_i(y_i-\mu_i)}{\phi\,V(\mu_i)}\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}x_{ij},
$$
using $a_i(\phi)=\phi/w_i$. This is @eq-glm-score. Collecting the summands into matrices with
$\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(a_i(\phi)V(\mu_i))$ gives the $j$-th component of
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu)$, which is
@eq-glm-score-matrix. The maximum likelihood estimator is an interior stationary point of the
differentiable concave-or-not log-likelihood, so it satisfies the first-order condition
$\mathbf U(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0$. Finally, every summand of @eq-glm-score carries the same
factor $1/\phi$, so $\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\phi^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf U}(\boldsymbol\beta)$ for a
$\phi$-free vector $\tilde{\mathbf U}$; the equation $\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf 0$ is equivalent
to $\tilde{\mathbf U}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf 0$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is unchanged by $\phi$.
$\square$
:::

The score equation has a transparent reading: $\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf 0$ requires the
covariate-weighted residuals $y_i-\mu_i$ to vanish, with each residual weighted by the local sensitivity
of the mean to the linear predictor and inversely by its variance. *Why this matters:* this is the GLM's
version of the orthogonality between residuals and the design columns that defined ordinary least squares
in Chapter 6, and it is the exact condition every fitting routine drives to zero. For the canonical link a
dramatic simplification occurs.

::: {#cor-canonical-score}
## Score equations under the canonical link
Under the canonical link, $d\mu_i/d\eta_i=V(\mu_i)$, and the score equations reduce to
$$
\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\frac{1}{\phi}\,\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W_0(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu)
\;\;\text{with}\;\;\mathbf W_0=\mathrm{diag}(w_i),
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(y_i-\mu_i)\,\mathbf x_i=\mathbf 0.
$$ {#eq-canonical-score}
In particular, if the model contains an intercept (a column of $\mathbf X$ equal to $\mathbf 1_n$), then
$\sum_i w_i\hat\mu_i=\sum_i w_iy_i$: the fitted values reproduce the response total exactly.
:::

::: {.proof}
With the canonical link $\eta_i=\theta_i$ by @prp-canonical-eta-theta, so
$d\mu_i/d\eta_i=d\mu_i/d\theta_i=b''(\theta_i)=V(\mu_i)$. Substituting into @eq-glm-score, the factor
$V(\mu_i)$ cancels:
$$
U_j(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_i\frac{w_i(y_i-\mu_i)}{\phi V(\mu_i)}V(\mu_i)x_{ij}
=\frac1\phi\sum_i w_i(y_i-\mu_i)x_{ij}.
$$
This is @eq-canonical-score. If a column of $\mathbf X$ is $\mathbf 1_n$, the corresponding component of
$\mathbf U(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0$ reads $\sum_i w_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)=0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## The logistic score in its familiar form
It is worth seeing @cor-canonical-score land on the textbook logistic score before meeting the general
machinery. For logistic regression the EDF member is the binomial proportion with weight $w_i=n_i$ and
mean $\mu_i=p_i$, so the canonical (logit) score equations read
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n n_i\,(y_i-p_i)\,\mathbf x_i=\mathbf 0:
$$
the covariate-weighted gap between observed proportions $y_i$ and fitted probabilities $p_i$ must vanish,
exactly the form quoted in introductory texts. With an intercept column this forces
$\sum_i n_i p_i=\sum_i n_i y_i=\sum_i R_i$, so the fitted model reproduces the total number of responders.
For the single arm of @exm-glm-running, an intercept-only fit solves $60\,(0.30-\hat p)=0$, returning
$\hat p=0.30$, the observed proportion. The general formula @eq-glm-score is just this familiar object
dressed for an arbitrary link and distribution. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Fisher information and Fisher scoring

To solve $\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf 0$ numerically we need the curvature of the
log-likelihood. We use the expected information rather than the observed Hessian, an algorithm due to
Fisher, because its form is especially clean.

::: {#prp-glm-information}
## Fisher information of a GLM
The Fisher information matrix (@def-fisher-information) of the GLM of @def-glm is
$$
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf W=\mathrm{diag}(W_i),
\quad
W_i=\frac{w_i}{\phi\,V(\mu_i)}\left(\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-glm-information}
The weights $W_i$ are positive, and $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)\succeq 0$, with
$\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)\succ 0$ whenever $\mathbf X$ has full column rank $p$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the information equality (@thm-information-equality), $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta))$.
From @eq-glm-score-matrix, $\mathbf U=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu)$,
where only $\mathbf y$ is random with $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf y)=\boldsymbol\Sigma$. Hence
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf U)
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\,\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf D\,\mathbf X
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf D\,\mathbf X,
$$
using that $\mathbf D$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ are diagonal hence symmetric. The diagonal matrix
$\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf D$ has $i$-th entry
$$
\frac{(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2}{a_i(\phi)V(\mu_i)}=\frac{w_i}{\phi V(\mu_i)}\left(\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}\right)^2=W_i,
$$
so $\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf D=\mathbf W$ and $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$.
Each $W_i>0$ because $w_i,\phi,V(\mu_i)>0$ and $d\mu_i/d\eta_i\neq0$ (the link is strictly monotone). For
any $\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^p$, $\mathbf v^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf v=\|\mathbf W^{1/2}\mathbf X\mathbf v\|_2^2\ge0$,
so $\mathcal I\succeq0$; it equals zero only if $\mathbf W^{1/2}\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$, i.e.
$\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ (as $\mathbf W^{1/2}$ is invertible), which forces $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$
when $\mathbf X$ has full column rank. The characterization of positive definiteness used here is
@thm-pd-characterization. $\square$
:::

*Why this matters.* The information matrix $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is the GLM's analogue of the
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ that governed precision in Chapter 6, now reweighted by the working weights
$\mathbf W$. Its inverse is the large-sample covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$
(@cor-glm-asymptotic-normality), so the diagonal entries of $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}$ are
the squared standard errors that a fitted model prints beside each coefficient. Curvature of the
log-likelihood becomes precision of the estimate; this is the bridge from the abstract Fisher information
to the standard error on a report.

The **Fisher scoring** algorithm is the Newton-type iteration that replaces the observed Hessian by its
expectation $\mathcal I$:
$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(m+1)}=\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}+\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)})^{-1}\,\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}).
$$ {#eq-fisher-scoring}
We now show that this iteration is exactly a weighted least squares fit, which is the content of the
acronym IRLS and the reason GLMs are computationally no harder than linear regression.

### Iteratively reweighted least squares

::: {#thm-irls}
## Iteratively reweighted least squares
The Fisher scoring update @eq-fisher-scoring for the GLM of @def-glm is identical to the weighted least
squares estimator
$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(m+1)}=\bigl(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf X\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf z^{(m)},
$$ {#eq-irls}
in which the **working weights** $\mathbf W^{(m)}=\mathrm{diag}(W_i^{(m)})$ are the information weights of
@eq-glm-information and the **working response** has components
$$
z_i^{(m)}=\eta_i^{(m)}+\bigl(y_i-\mu_i^{(m)}\bigr)\,\frac{d\eta_i}{d\mu_i}\bigg|^{(m)}
=\eta_i^{(m)}+\bigl(y_i-\mu_i^{(m)}\bigr)\,g'(\mu_i^{(m)}),
$$ {#eq-working-response}
all quantities evaluated at $\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}$. Each iteration is therefore the solution of the
weighted normal equations $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf X\,\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf z^{(m)}$
of Chapter 6 applied to the data $(\mathbf z^{(m)},\mathbf X)$ with weights $\mathbf W^{(m)}$. The common
factor $1/\phi$ in $\mathbf W^{(m)}$ cancels between $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf X)^{-1}$ and
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}$, so neither the iterates nor their limit $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ depend
on $\phi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathbf D=\mathrm{diag}(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)$, evaluated at $\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}$, and recall from
the proof of @prp-glm-information that $\mathbf W=\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf D$, hence
$\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}=\mathbf W\mathbf D^{-1}$ (all factors diagonal and invertible). By
@eq-glm-score-matrix the score is
$$
\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)})=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\,\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu^{(m)})
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\,\mathbf D^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu^{(m)}).
$$
The diagonal matrix $\mathbf D^{-1}$ has $i$-th entry $d\eta_i/d\mu_i=g'(\mu_i)$, so
$\mathbf D^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu^{(m)})$ has $i$-th entry
$(y_i-\mu_i^{(m)})g'(\mu_i^{(m)})=z_i^{(m)}-\eta_i^{(m)}$ by @eq-working-response. Therefore
$$
\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)})=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\,(\mathbf z^{(m)}-\boldsymbol\eta^{(m)}),
\qquad\boldsymbol\eta^{(m)}=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}.
$$
Insert this and $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)})=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ (@eq-glm-information)
into the Fisher scoring update @eq-fisher-scoring:
$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(m+1)}
=\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}+(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W(\mathbf z^{(m)}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}).
$$
Now $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}=\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}$,
so the two $\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}$ terms cancel:
$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(m+1)}=\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}+(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf z^{(m)}-\boldsymbol\beta^{(m)}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf z^{(m)},
$$
which is @eq-irls. This is the weighted least squares solution because it solves the weighted normal
equations $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf z^{(m)}$,
the weighted analogue of @thm-ols-normal-equations. Writing $\mathbf W^{(m)}=\phi^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf W}^{(m)}$
with $\tilde{\mathbf W}^{(m)}$ free of $\phi$, the scalar $\phi^{-1}$ multiplies both
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(m)}\mathbf z^{(m)}$ and cancels in
@eq-irls. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## IRLS in words, and why it is a sequence of linear regressions
The algorithm @eq-irls says: given a current coefficient guess, form a synthetic response $\mathbf z$ by
taking the current linear predictor and adding the raw residual rescaled to the linear-predictor scale,
attach the weight $W_i$ to observation $i$, run an ordinary weighted linear regression of $\mathbf z$ on
$\mathbf X$, and repeat until the coefficients stop changing. Because each step is a weighted projection
of $\mathbf z$ onto $\mathcal C(\mathbf X)$ in the $\mathbf W$-inner product (@def-hat-matrix), every tool
of Chapter 6, the hat matrix, leverages, and the standard-error formula, transfers verbatim to the final
iteration. This is why fitting a logistic or Poisson regression costs no more than a handful of linear
regressions, and why GLM software is built on a linear-algebra core. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## One IRLS step, with numbers
To watch the machinery move before meeting more theory, take the two-group logistic data of
@sec-glm-worked ($R_1=2$ of $n_1=10$ at $x=0$; $R_2=7$ of $n_2=10$ at $x=1$) and start from
$\boldsymbol\beta^{(0)}=(0,0)^\top$, so every fitted probability is $p_i^{(0)}=\tfrac12$. The recipe of
@eq-working-response and @eq-glm-information gives, for group $1$, a working response
$z_1=0+(0.2-0.5)/(0.5\cdot0.5)=-1.2$ and a working weight $W_1=n_1p(1-p)=10(0.25)=2.5$, and likewise
$z_2=0.8$, $W_2=2.5$. A single weighted least squares fit of the synthetic response
$\mathbf z=(-1.2,\,0.8)^\top$ on $\mathbf X$ with these weights returns
$\boldsymbol\beta^{(1)}=(-1.2,\,2.0)^\top$, already most of the way to the maximum likelihood value
$(-1.386,\,2.234)$. That is the whole algorithm in one line: build $\mathbf z$, attach the weights, run one
linear regression, repeat. The full iteration and its convergence are carried out in @sec-glm-worked.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

For the canonical link the algorithm has a further property: Fisher scoring coincides with the exact
Newton-Raphson method, because the observed and expected information agree.

::: {#lem-canonical-hessian}
## Canonical link: observed equals expected information, and concavity
Under the canonical link the Hessian of the log-likelihood is the nonrandom matrix
$$
\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=-\,\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X=-\,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta),
$$
so the observed information equals the expected information and Fisher scoring @eq-fisher-scoring is
Newton-Raphson. Consequently $\ell$ is concave in $\boldsymbol\beta$, and strictly concave when
$\mathbf X$ has full column rank, so a stationary point is the unique global maximizer.
:::

::: {.proof}
Under the canonical link, $\eta_i=\theta_i$ (@prp-canonical-eta-theta), so @eq-glm-loglik becomes
$\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_i(y_i\eta_i-b(\eta_i))/a_i(\phi)$ with $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$.
Differentiating twice,
$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_j}=\sum_i\frac{(y_i-b'(\eta_i))x_{ij}}{a_i(\phi)},
\qquad
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\beta_j\partial\beta_k}=-\sum_i\frac{b''(\eta_i)x_{ij}x_{ik}}{a_i(\phi)}.
$$
Because $b''(\eta_i)=V(\mu_i)$ and $a_i(\phi)=\phi/w_i$, the $i$-th coefficient is
$w_iV(\mu_i)/\phi=W_i$ (the canonical-link weight, since $d\mu_i/d\eta_i=V(\mu_i)$ makes
$W_i=w_iV(\mu_i)^2/(\phi V(\mu_i))=w_iV(\mu_i)/\phi$). Hence
$\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=-\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X=-\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta)$. This
matrix does not involve $\mathbf y$, so the observed information $-\nabla^2\ell$ equals the expected
information $\mathcal I$, and the Newton step $-(\nabla^2\ell)^{-1}\mathbf U=\mathcal I^{-1}\mathbf U$ is
the Fisher scoring step. Since $\mathcal I=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\succeq0$ by
@prp-glm-information, $\nabla^2\ell\preceq0$ and $\ell$ is concave; full column rank gives
$\mathcal I\succ0$, strict concavity, and uniqueness of the maximizer. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## When the maximizer fails to exist: separation
Strict concavity guarantees the maximizer is unique *if it exists*, but for logistic regression it may
fail to exist. If a hyperplane $\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta=0$ perfectly separates the successes from
the failures, the likelihood increases without bound as $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|\to\infty$ along the
separating direction, and the IRLS weights $W_i=n_ip_i(1-p_i)\to0$. For a concrete health-data instance,
take a subgroup table in which all $8$ treated patients respond and none of the $6$ controls do: the
fitted treated odds are $8/0$, the estimated log odds ratio marches off to $+\infty$, and no finite
$\hat\beta_1$ solves the score equation. This is **complete separation**; the
finite-sample maximum likelihood estimator does not exist, even though the population parameter is
perfectly well defined. The phenomenon is benign in large randomized trials but common in sparse
subgroup tables, and it motivates the penalized and Bayesian fits of Chapter 8. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Overdispersion: where the dispersion re-enters
@thm-glm-score showed that $\phi$ cancels from the estimating equation, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is the
same whether the binomial or Poisson dispersion takes its nominal value $\phi=1$ or not. That does not
make $\phi$ irrelevant. Real trial and count data are often **overdispersed**: the observed spread of the
proportions or counts exceeds the $V(\mu)=\mu(1-\mu)$ or $V(\mu)=\mu$ that the family mandates, usually
because of unmodeled heterogeneity between patients or clusters (extra-binomial or extra-Poisson
variation). The point estimates $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ remain valid, but the model-based standard errors
from $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}$, computed as if $\phi=1$, are then too small. The standard
remedies estimate a free dispersion $\hat\phi>1$ and inflate every standard error by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$
(quasi-likelihood), or move to a genuinely overdispersed model such as the negative binomial or a
random-effects GLM, the latter being the subject of Chapter 8. The one thing overdispersion never does is
change which $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ solves the score equation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Large-sample distribution of the estimator

The estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is a maximum likelihood estimator of a regular parametric model,
so its large-sample behavior is governed by the general theorem of Chapter 5. We state the specialization
and verify its hypotheses.

::: {#cor-glm-asymptotic-normality}
## Asymptotic normality of the GLM estimator
Consider the GLM of @def-glm with true coefficient $\boldsymbol\beta_0$, fixed dimension $p$, and design
sequence such that $\frac1n\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W(\boldsymbol\beta_0)\mathbf X\to\mathbf A$ for a positive
definite limit $\mathbf A$, with the regularity conditions (A1) to (A3) of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality
holding (they do for the canonical link with full column rank by @lem-canonical-hessian). Then the
maximum likelihood estimator satisfies
$$
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta_0)\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\mathcal N_p\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\;\mathbf A^{-1}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-glm-asymptotic-normality}
and in the working finite-sample form
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\;\dot\sim\;\mathcal N_p\!\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_0,\,(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}\bigr)$.
A standard error for $\hat\beta_j$ is the square root of the $(j,j)$ entry of
$(\mathbf X^\top\hat{\mathbf W}\mathbf X)^{-1}$, with $\hat{\mathbf W}=\mathbf W(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$.
:::

*Why this matters.* This corollary is the reason a fitted GLM reports more than a point estimate. The
limiting covariance $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}$ is exactly what statistical software returns
as the squared standard errors next to each coefficient, and exponentiating a Wald interval for
$\hat\beta_j$ (the next remark) is how the same software produces the confidence interval for an odds
ratio or rate ratio that a meta-analysis then carries forward. Without this theorem an estimate would be a
bare number with no measure of its uncertainty, and no indirect comparison could be built on it.

::: {.proof}
The GLM is a parametric model with log-likelihood @eq-glm-loglik, score
$\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf D\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu)$
(@thm-glm-score), and Fisher information $\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$
(@prp-glm-information), where the subscript $n$ records that this is the information in all $n$
observations. The per-observation scores are independent with mean zero (by @thm-glm-score each summand
of @eq-glm-score has expectation $\propto\mathbb E[y_i-\mu_i]=0$) and finite covariance, so the
hypotheses of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality are exactly the stated regularity conditions. For the
canonical link, @lem-canonical-hessian shows the Hessian is the constant matrix
$-\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$, so condition (A3) (a local uniform law for the Hessian) holds
trivially and the model is regular on a neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\beta_0$; condition (A2) is
$\mathbf A\succ0$. Applying @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality with total information
$\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0)$ and the scaling
$\frac1n\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0)=\frac1n\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\to\mathbf A$ yields
@eq-glm-asymptotic-normality. The finite-sample statement substitutes $\mathcal I_n^{-1}=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)^{-1}$
for $\frac1n\mathbf A^{-1}$, and consistency of $\hat{\mathbf W}$ for $\mathbf W(\boldsymbol\beta_0)$
(continuity of $\mathbf W(\cdot)$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\beta_0$) with the
continuous mapping theorem justifies the plug-in standard error. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Standard errors for odds ratios and rate ratios
The reported effect is usually not $\hat\beta_j$ but the odds ratio $e^{\hat\beta_j}$ or rate ratio
$e^{\hat\beta_j}$. By the delta method (@thm-delta-method) with $h(\beta)=e^\beta$ and $h'(\beta)=e^\beta$,
$$
\mathrm{SE}\bigl(e^{\hat\beta_j}\bigr)\approx e^{\hat\beta_j}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta_j),
$$
and a confidence interval for the odds ratio is obtained by exponentiating the endpoints of a Wald
interval for $\beta_j$, which respects the positivity of the ratio. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Why this matters for indirect comparison
Everything in this section runs once per trial arm when an indirect comparison is assembled. The score
equation locates each arm's fitted log-odds or log-rate; iteratively reweighted least squares computes it
at the cost of a few linear regressions; the asymptotic theory attaches a standard error to it. A network
meta-analysis then treats those per-arm link-scale effects, with their standard errors, as the data it
combines (Chapters 13 to 15). The estimation machinery here is therefore not a detour: it is the exact
procedure that turns a stack of trial two-by-two tables into the log odds ratios and variances the later
chapters pool. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Deviance {#sec-deviance}

The residual sum of squares of Chapter 6 measured the misfit of a linear model and drove its
$F$-tests. Its GLM generalization is the **deviance**, and the idea behind it is a direct translation of
that story. In a linear model, misfit is the squared gap between the data and the fit; in a GLM, where the
response need not be normal, the natural currency of fit is not squared error but log-likelihood, so we
measure misfit by how far the fitted model's log-likelihood falls short of the best any model in the
family could achieve on this data. That best is the **saturated model**, which fits every observation
exactly. Twice the log-likelihood gap between the saturated fit and our fit is the deviance: it is
nonnegative, it is zero exactly when the fit is perfect, and (as @prp-deviance-nonneg will show) for the
normal linear model it equals the residual sum of squares outright, so the deviance genuinely extends
Chapter 6 rather than replacing it. Differences of deviances between nested models then test whether added
covariates improve fit, the GLM version of the extra-sum-of-squares $F$-test. We build these objects in
order: the saturated model, the deviance itself, its nonnegativity, and finally the model-comparison test.

::: {#def-saturated-model}
## Saturated model
The **saturated model** for responses $y_1,\dots,y_n$ is the GLM with one free mean parameter per
observation, fitted at $\tilde\mu_i=y_i$ for every $i$, with natural parameter
$\tilde\theta_i=\theta(y_i)$. It attains the largest log-likelihood achievable by any model in the family
for the given data, because each term $y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)$ in @eq-glm-loglik is maximized over
$\theta_i$ where its derivative vanishes, $\frac{d}{d\theta_i}\bigl[y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)\bigr]=y_i-b'(\theta_i)=0$,
that is at $b'(\theta_i)=y_i$, i.e. at $\theta_i=\tilde\theta_i$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-deviance}
## Deviance and residual deviance
Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ be the fitted coefficients of a GLM, with fitted means $\hat\mu_i$ and
natural parameters $\hat\theta_i=\theta(\hat\mu_i)$. The **scaled deviance** is twice the log-likelihood
gap between the saturated model and the fitted model,
$$
D^\ast(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})=2\bigl[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}(\mathbf y)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\bigr]
=\frac{2}{\phi}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\Bigl[y_i(\tilde\theta_i-\hat\theta_i)-b(\tilde\theta_i)+b(\hat\theta_i)\Bigr],
$$ {#eq-scaled-deviance}
and the **deviance** is its dispersion-free numerator
$$
D(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})=\phi\,D^\ast(\mathbf y;\hat{\boldsymbol\mu})
=2\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\Bigl[y_i(\tilde\theta_i-\hat\theta_i)-b(\tilde\theta_i)+b(\hat\theta_i)\Bigr]
=\sum_{i=1}^n d_i.
$$ {#eq-deviance}
The value of $D$ at the fitted model is the **residual deviance**; the **deviance residual** of
observation $i$ is $r_i^D=\mathrm{sign}(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\sqrt{d_i}$, so that $\sum_i(r_i^D)^2=D$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* The deviance is one number saying how far the fitted model sits from a flawless fit:
large deviance, poor fit; zero deviance, perfect fit. The **scaled** deviance simply divides by the
dispersion $\phi$ (for the binomial and Poisson $\phi=1$, so the two coincide). The **deviance residuals**
$r_i^D$ are the GLM's stand-ins for the ordinary residuals $y_i-\hat\mu_i$ of Chapter 6: they carry the
sign of the raw residual, and their squares sum to the total deviance, exactly as squared residuals summed
to the residual sum of squares.

::: {.remark}
## Bregman divergence (a named building block)
The proof of the next proposition uses one recurring construction, so we name it once here rather than
mid-argument. For a smooth strictly convex function $b$, the **Bregman divergence** from $v$ to $u$ is
$$
D_b(u,v)=b(u)-b(v)-b'(v)(u-v),
$$
the gap at the point $u$ between $b$ itself and its tangent line drawn at $v$. Because a convex function
lies on or above each of its tangents, $D_b(u,v)\ge0$, with equality only when $u=v$; this single
inequality is what forces the deviance to be nonnegative. No prior acquaintance with the term is assumed:
it is just a name for "function minus its own tangent line." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-deviance-nonneg}
## The deviance is a sum of nonnegative Bregman divergences
Each deviance contribution satisfies $d_i\ge0$, with $d_i=0$ if and only if $\hat\mu_i=y_i$. Hence
$D\ge0$, and $D=0$ if and only if the fit is saturated. For the normal linear model with identity link,
$D=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2$ is the residual sum of squares of Chapter 6.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $i$ and write $u=\hat\theta_i$, $v=\tilde\theta_i$. Since $\tilde\mu_i=y_i=b'(\tilde\theta_i)=b'(v)$,
$$
\tfrac12\,d_i/w_i=y_i(v-u)-b(v)+b(u)=b'(v)(v-u)-b(v)+b(u)=b(u)-b(v)-b'(v)(u-v)=:D_b(u,v).
$$
The quantity $D_b(u,v)$ is exactly the Bregman divergence of the convex function $b$ just defined: by
Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder there is $\xi$ between $u$ and $v$ with
$D_b(u,v)=\tfrac12 b''(\xi)(u-v)^2\ge0$, since $b''>0$. It is zero exactly when $u=v$, i.e.
$\hat\theta_i=\tilde\theta_i$, equivalently $\hat\mu_i=b'(\hat\theta_i)=b'(\tilde\theta_i)=y_i$. Thus
$d_i=2w_iD_b(u,v)\ge0$ with equality iff $\hat\mu_i=y_i$, and summing gives $D\ge0$ with equality iff the
fit is saturated. For the normal model $b(\theta)=\theta^2/2$, $\theta=\mu$, $w_i=1$, so
$d_i=2[y_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)-\tfrac12y_i^2+\tfrac12\hat\mu_i^2]=y_i^2-2y_i\hat\mu_i+\hat\mu_i^2=(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2$,
and $D=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2=\mathrm{RSS}$. $\square$
:::

The deviance specializes to clean closed forms for the discrete families, which are the ones used in
practice.

::: {#exm-deviance-forms}
## Poisson and binomial deviance
**Poisson.** With $b(\theta)=e^\theta$, $\theta=\log\mu$, $w_i=1$, the $i$-th contribution is
$d_i=2[y_i\log y_i-y_i-y_i\log\hat\mu_i+\hat\mu_i]=2[y_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)]$, so
$$
D_{\mathrm{Poisson}}=2\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl[y_i\log\frac{y_i}{\hat\mu_i}-(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\Bigr],
$$
with the convention $0\log0=0$. If the model has an intercept then $\sum_i\hat\mu_i=\sum_iy_i$ by
@cor-canonical-score, and the second term vanishes, leaving $D=2\sum_iy_i\log(y_i/\hat\mu_i)$.

**Binomial proportion.** With $y_i=R_i/n_i$, $\hat\mu_i=\hat p_i$, $w_i=n_i$, and writing the fitted
counts $\hat R_i=n_i\hat p_i$, the contribution is
$d_i=2n_i[y_i\log(y_i/\hat p_i)+(1-y_i)\log((1-y_i)/(1-\hat p_i))]$, so in count form
$$
D_{\mathrm{binom}}=2\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigl[R_i\log\frac{R_i}{\hat R_i}+(n_i-R_i)\log\frac{n_i-R_i}{n_i-\hat R_i}\Bigr].
$$
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Deviance for model comparison

The deviance is to GLMs what the residual sum of squares is to linear models: the basis of the
goodness-of-fit and nested-model tests. The key fact is that a difference of scaled deviances is exactly
a likelihood ratio statistic.

::: {#thm-deviance-test}
## Analysis of deviance
Let $M_0\subset M_1$ be nested GLMs with the same EDF, the same link, and the same known dispersion
$\phi$, with $p_0<p_1$ parameters, fitted by maximum likelihood with residual deviances $D_0\ge D_1$.
Then the scaled deviance difference equals the likelihood ratio statistic for $M_0$ within $M_1$,
$$
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}=2\bigl[\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)\bigr],
$$ {#eq-deviance-diff}
and under $M_0$, as $n\to\infty$,
$$
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^2_{\,p_1-p_0}.
$$ {#eq-deviance-chisq}
When $\phi$ is unknown (as for the normal or gamma families) it is replaced by a consistent estimator
$\hat\phi$ and $(D_0-D_1)/\{\hat\phi(p_1-p_0)\}$ is referred to an $F_{p_1-p_0,\,n-p_1}$ distribution.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-scaled-deviance the scaled deviance of a model is $D^\ast=2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})]$,
and the saturated log-likelihood $\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}(\mathbf y)$ does not depend on which fitted model
is used. Subtracting,
$$
\frac{D_0-D_1}{\phi}=D_0^\ast-D_1^\ast
=2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)]-2[\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)]
=2[\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_1)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_0)],
$$
which is @eq-deviance-diff: the saturated term cancels and what remains is twice the maximized
log-likelihood gap between the two models, i.e. the log likelihood ratio statistic for testing $M_0$
inside $M_1$. Under $M_0$ this statistic converges in distribution to $\chi^2_{p_1-p_0}$ by Wilks's
theorem (@thm-wilks), the number of degrees of freedom being the difference $p_1-p_0$ in the number of
free parameters. The $F$ reference distribution for unknown $\phi$ follows from writing the statistic as
a ratio of the deviance difference to an independent estimator of $\phi$ scaled by its degrees of
freedom, exactly as the linear-model $F$-test of Chapter 6 arises from the ratio of two sums of squares.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
## Reading an analysis-of-deviance table
Theorem @thm-deviance-test licenses the standard workflow: fit a sequence of nested models, tabulate
their residual deviances, and test each added term by referring the drop in deviance to a chi-square (or
$F$) distribution on the added degrees of freedom. This is the GLM counterpart of the analysis-of-variance
$F$-test used for the linear model of Chapter 6: the drop in deviance plays the role of the extra
regression sum of squares, and for the normal family with the identity link the deviance test reduces to
exactly that $F$-test. The residual deviance of a single model, compared to
its degrees of freedom $n-p$, is itself a rough absolute goodness-of-fit check, because under a
correctly specified model with $\phi$ known the residual deviance is approximately $\chi^2_{n-p}$ in
favorable (large per-group count) regimes. The worked example of @sec-glm-worked carries this out by
hand. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and the hazard ratio {#sec-noncollapsibility}

We now reach the phenomenon that distinguishes nonlinear-link GLMs from the linear model and that
reverberates through the rest of the book. In a linear model the coefficient of a treatment indicator is
both the effect within every covariate stratum and the effect on the population average, because
expectation is linear. For the odds ratio and the hazard ratio this is false: an effect that is constant
across strata need not equal the effect computed from the population-averaged risks. The marginal and the
conditional effect are different numbers, and the difference is not bias from confounding but an
arithmetic consequence of the nonlinearity of the link.

To see why the linear model is the special case, write the marginal treatment effect on the identity
scale as the average of the stratum-specific effects. With no confounding,
$$
\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]-\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]=\mathbb E_X\bigl[\mu_1(X)-\mu_0(X)\bigr]=\delta,
$$
so if the within-stratum difference is a constant $\delta$, the population-average difference is that same
$\delta$. Linearity of the expectation is doing all the work; the odds ratio and hazard ratio break
precisely because their scales are nonlinear.

For a health researcher the phenomenon is concrete before it is formal. Suppose a trial reports a
conditional odds ratio of $3.5$ for an active drug versus control, and that this same $3.5$ holds in both
younger and older patients, so there is no effect modification by age. Yet when the two age groups are
pooled and a single odds ratio is computed from the combined response rates, the answer is about $3.14$,
not $3.5$. Nothing was confounded and no subgroup interaction was hidden; the pooled number simply differs
from the common stratum number by arithmetic. The whole of this section formalizes that observation, and
its consequence for a systematic review is immediate: an odds ratio reported by a trial is a *conditional*
effect tied to the covariates in that trial's model, whereas an indirect comparison may need a *marginal*
effect for a target population, and the two are not interchangeable even under flawless randomization. The
numbers $3.5$ and $3.14$ reappear, computed exactly, in @exm-noncollapsible-or.

### A precise definition

We work with two treatments, indexed by the potential outcomes $Y(0),Y(1)$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd), and a
baseline covariate $X$ that stratifies the population. Write $\mu_t(x)=\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid X=x]$ for the
stratum-specific mean outcome under treatment $t$, and assume throughout this section the no-confounding
identity $\mathbb E[Y(t)]=\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)]$, so that the marginal mean is the average of the
conditional means. We compare effects measured on the scale of a strictly increasing transform $g$, the
effect measure's link (logit for the odds ratio).

::: {#def-non-collapsibility}
## Collapsibility and non-collapsibility of an effect measure
For a strictly increasing transform $g$ define the **conditional effect** in stratum $x$ and the
**marginal effect** by
$$
\psi_g(x)=g(\mu_1(x))-g(\mu_0(x)),
\qquad
\psi_g^{\mathrm M}=g\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\mu_1(X)]\bigr)-g\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\mu_0(X)]\bigr).
$$ {#eq-cond-marg-effect}
The effect measure based on $g$ is **collapsible** over $X$ if, whenever the conditional effect is
constant in $x$ (no effect modification on the $g$-scale), $\psi_g(x)\equiv\psi_g$, the marginal effect
equals that common value, $\psi_g^{\mathrm M}=\psi_g$, for every distribution of $X$ and every pair of
stratum means $\mu_0(\cdot),\mu_1(\cdot)$ consistent with it. The measure is **non-collapsible** if it is
not collapsible, that is, if there exist stratum means with constant conditional effect for which
$\psi_g^{\mathrm M}\neq\psi_g$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::
